_meta.description: Quiz questions for Project Amazon PH Academy modules. Each quiz maps to a module's final lesson (knowledge check). Questions test PPC concepts covered in the preceding lessons.

quizzes.title: Onboarding Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of the Project Amazon PH Academy platform and Amazon PPC basics covered in the Onboarding module.

questions.question: What does PPC stand for in the context of Amazon advertising?
questions.optionA: Pay Per Click
questions.optionB: Product Promotion Campaign
questions.optionC: Paid Product Catalog
questions.optionD: Performance Per Cost
questions.explanation: PPC stands for Pay Per Click — you only pay when a shopper clicks on your ad, not when it's displayed.

questions.question: Which Amazon ad type appears within search results and on product detail pages?
questions.optionA: Sponsored Brands
questions.optionB: Sponsored Display
questions.optionC: Sponsored Products
questions.optionD: Display Ads
questions.explanation: Sponsored Products are the most common ad type — they appear in search results and on product detail pages, promoting individual listings.

questions.question: What is the primary benefit of Amazon PPC for sellers?
questions.optionA: Free product listings on Amazon
questions.optionB: Increased organic search ranking guaranteed
questions.optionC: Getting products in front of shoppers who are actively searching
questions.optionD: Automatic review generation
questions.explanation: Amazon PPC puts your products in front of shoppers who are actively searching for related items, giving you visibility at the moment of purchase intent.

questions.question: What does your Amazon PPC bid actually control?
questions.optionA: The exact price you'll pay for every click
questions.optionB: A starting point that placement adjustments and your bid strategy then act on to set the real ceiling
questions.optionC: A price that never changes once the campaign is live
questions.optionD: A guaranteed discount of one cent below the next bidder
questions.explanation: Your entered bid is the base. Placement adjustments raise it for specific placements, and your bid strategy setting decides whether the result is a hard ceiling (Fixed Bids, Dynamic Down Only) or something Amazon can raise further for likely conversions (Dynamic Up and Down). The safe habit isn't memorizing an auction formula, it's setting a defensible maximum bid and then watching your realized CPC in the reports.

questions.question: What should you do before launching your first Amazon PPC campaign?
questions.optionA: Set the highest possible bids to win all auctions
questions.optionB: Make sure your product listing is optimized with good images and copy
questions.optionC: Wait until you have at least 100 reviews
questions.optionD: Only target the most expensive keywords
questions.explanation: Your product listing is the foundation of PPC success. Even the best ads can't convert if the listing is poor. Optimize images, title, bullets, and price before spending on ads.

quizzes.title: PPC Foundations Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Verify your mastery of the core PPC metrics — CPC, CTR, ACoS, TACoS, and RoAS — the building blocks of every Amazon advertising decision.

questions.question: If you spend $200 on a keyword and receive 160 clicks, what is your CPC?
questions.explanation: CPC = Total Spend / Total Clicks = $200 / 160 = $1.25. This is your average cost for each click received.

questions.question: Your ad receives 3,000 impressions and 90 clicks. What is the CTR?
questions.explanation: CTR = Clicks / Impressions = 90 / 3,000 = 0.03 = 3.0%. A 3% CTR is solid for exact match keywords on Amazon.

questions.question: What does ACoS measure?
questions.optionA: The percentage of clicks that result in a sale
questions.optionB: The ratio of ad spend to ad revenue
questions.optionC: The total advertising cost of your entire account
questions.optionD: The average cost per sale across all campaigns
questions.explanation: ACoS (Advertising Cost of Sales) = Ad Spend / Ad Revenue. It tells you what percentage of your ad revenue goes toward ad costs. A 25% ACoS means you spend $0.25 on ads for every $1 in ad revenue.

questions.question: How is TACoS different from ACoS?
questions.optionA: TACoS includes organic sales in the denominator, ACoS only uses ad revenue
questions.optionB: TACoS is always higher than ACoS
questions.optionC: They measure the same thing — TACoS is just the newer name
questions.optionD: TACoS measures click cost while ACoS measures revenue
questions.explanation: TACoS = Ad Spend / Total Revenue (organic + ads), while ACoS = Ad Spend / Ad Revenue only. TACoS shows how ads impact your whole business, not just the direct ad-attributed revenue.

questions.question: A keyword has an ACoS of 45% and your product profit margin is 30%. What should you consider?
questions.optionA: The keyword is performing well — keep it as-is
questions.optionB: You're likely losing money on this keyword since ACoS exceeds profit margin
questions.optionC: The profit margin doesn't matter for ACoS calculations
questions.optionD: You should double your bid to get more clicks
questions.explanation: When ACoS exceeds your profit margin, you're spending more on ads than you make in profit. A 45% ACoS on a 30% margin means you lose 15 percentage points on every ad-attributed sale. Consider lowering bids, adding negatives, or pausing.

questions.question: If your RoAS is 4.0x, what does that mean?
questions.optionA: You get 4 clicks for every dollar spent
questions.optionB: You earn $4 in total revenue for every $1 spent on ads
questions.optionC: You earn $4 in ad revenue for every $1 spent on ads
questions.optionD: Your ACoS is 4%
questions.explanation: RoAS = Ad Revenue / Ad Spend. A 4.0x RoAS means for every $1 in ad spend, you generate $4 in ad-attributed revenue. It's the inverse of ACoS: RoAS = 1 / ACoS.

questions.question: Why is it dangerous to evaluate CPC in isolation?
questions.optionA: CPC is not an important metric
questions.optionB: A low CPC on irrelevant keywords can still waste money if those clicks don't convert
questions.optionC: Amazon doesn't report CPC accurately
questions.optionD: CPC should always be as low as possible regardless of other metrics
questions.explanation: Cheap clicks from irrelevant search terms can have a low CPC but infinite effective cost if they never convert. Always evaluate CPC alongside CVR, ACoS, and relevance.

questions.question: What is the relationship between CTR and CPC in Amazon's advertising system?
questions.optionA: They are completely independent metrics
questions.optionB: Higher CTR can lead to lower CPC because Amazon rewards relevant ads
questions.optionC: Higher CTR always means higher CPC
questions.optionD: CTR only affects ad placement, not CPC
questions.explanation: Amazon's algorithm uses CTR as a quality signal. Higher CTR indicates relevance, which can lead to better placements at lower costs, creating a virtuous cycle of better performance.

questions.question: A campaign has a strong 3.2% CTR but only a 1.5% CVR, and ACoS is well above margin. What's the most defensible first action?
questions.optionA: Lower the bid immediately to cut spend
questions.optionB: Pull the search-term report to confirm relevance, then inspect the listing
questions.optionC: Pause the keyword since it clearly isn't working
questions.optionD: Raise the bid to get more data faster
questions.explanation: High CTR with low CVR usually points to a listing problem once you've confirmed the traffic is relevant, not a targeting or bid problem. Cutting the bid or pausing the keyword first risks losing traffic that would convert if the listing were fixed.

questions.question: A campaign launched 8 days ago is running a 65% ACoS on a product with a 35% margin. What's the most useful next question?
questions.optionA: Is this campaign a failure that should be paused?
questions.optionB: Is ACoS trending down week over week as the campaign gathers data?
questions.optionC: Should the bid be doubled to win more auctions faster?
questions.optionD: Is 65% ACoS acceptable forever since it's a new product?
questions.explanation: New campaigns often run high ACoS while they build search-term data and reviews. The useful question isn't whether today's number is high, it's whether the trend is moving toward break-even. Judge launch campaigns on trajectory, not one day's number.

questions.question: TACoS has risen from 15% to 22% over the past month while ACoS stayed flat. What should you check before telling the client organic sales are falling?
questions.optionA: Nothing — a rising TACoS always means organic sales are falling
questions.optionB: The actual ad-sales and organic-sales split behind the total
questions.optionC: Whether the client's return policy changed
questions.optionD: The campaign's placement adjustments only
questions.explanation: A rising TACoS with flat ACoS can come from falling organic sales, but also from total sales staying flat while ad spend grows, or a seasonal dip. Pull the ad-sales and organic-sales split before naming a cause.

questions.question: Amazon's suggested bid range for a keyword is $0.90 to $1.30. Your calculated maximum CPC for the target ACoS is $0.60. What should you do?
questions.optionA: Bid within Amazon's suggested range since Amazon knows the auction best
questions.optionB: Treat the suggested range as a signal to compare against your maximum, and bid at or below what your numbers support
questions.optionC: Split the difference between the suggested range and your maximum
questions.optionD: Ignore your maximum CPC calculation since Amazon's suggestion is more current
questions.explanation: Amazon's suggested bid reflects what tends to win the auction, not what your margin can afford. When the suggested range sits above your maximum CPC, hold your bid near your own ceiling and investigate targeting or listing fixes instead of chasing the suggestion.

quizzes.title: Keyword Research Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of match types, keyword research workflow, negative keywords, and keyword grouping.

questions.question: What's the main difference between broad match and exact match keywords?
questions.optionA: Broad match shows ads for a wide range of related searches; exact match shows ads only for the precise term or very close variants
questions.optionB: Broad match is always cheaper per click than exact match
questions.optionC: Exact match shows ads for related searches; broad match only matches the literal term
questions.optionD: There is no functional difference, only a naming difference
questions.explanation: Broad match casts the widest net and can trigger on related searches Amazon judges relevant. Exact match is the tightest control, showing your ad only for the precise term or very close variants.

questions.question: A search term surfacing under one of your broader keywords gets 200 clicks and $150 in ad spend, with $0 in sales. What's the right read?
questions.optionA: Its ACoS (advertising cost of sales, ad spend divided by ad sales) is 100%, which is acceptable
questions.optionB: It's a strong candidate to add as a negative keyword. With zero sales, ACoS is undefined, not a fixed percentage, and this spend is pure waste
questions.optionC: It should be given a higher bid to try to generate a sale
questions.optionD: Nothing needs to change since spend is under $200
questions.explanation: ACoS is spend divided by sales, which is undefined at $0 in sales, not 100%. 200 clicks and $150 spent with zero orders on this search term is a clear signal to add it as a negative so it stops draining budget under your broader keyword.

questions.question: Which two match types can you actually use for negative keywords on Amazon?
questions.optionA: Negative broad and negative phrase
questions.optionB: Negative exact and negative broad
questions.optionC: Negative phrase and negative exact
questions.optionD: Negative broad only
questions.explanation: Amazon supports negative phrase and negative exact match. There's no negative broad match, so you can't block an entire loose category of searches with a single negative the way broad match works for regular targeting.

questions.question: Your keyword research turns up 500 candidate keywords for one product. What should you do before adding them to a campaign?
questions.optionA: Add all 500 immediately. More keywords always means more sales
questions.optionB: Score and filter them for relevance and likely volume first, then launch with the strongest subset
questions.optionC: Only use the 5 most expensive keywords
questions.optionD: Wait until you have Brand Registry before adding any keywords
questions.explanation: Unfiltered keyword lists bring in irrelevant traffic and make performance data harder to read. Score candidates for relevance and volume, launch with the strongest set, then expand from real data.

questions.question: Why does it make sense to shift more budget toward exact-match keywords once you have performance data on them?
questions.optionA: Exact match keywords with a proven conversion history are your most predictable, lowest-risk spend
questions.optionB: Exact match is always required by Amazon once a campaign has run for 30 days
questions.optionC: Exact match keywords are always cheaper per click than broad or phrase
questions.optionD: Broad match keywords stop working after enough data accumulates
questions.explanation: Once an exact-match keyword has a real conversion track record, it's the most predictable place to invest further budget. Broad and phrase remain useful for discovering new terms, not for scaling proven ones.

questions.question: An ad group has "cutting board for meat," "cutting board gift set," and "large cutting board." What's the problem with this grouping?
questions.optionA: There's no problem — they're all cutting board keywords
questions.optionB: The keywords reflect three different shopper intents (use case, gift buying, size), so one bid and one negative list won't fit all three well
questions.optionC: The group has too few keywords to be useful
questions.optionD: Match types are mixed, which is the only real grouping error
questions.explanation: A good ad group shares one obvious shopper intent so a single bid and negative list make sense for everything in it. A gift buyer, a use-case buyer, and a size-driven buyer are different shoppers behind the same product, and grouping them together blurs the bid and reporting clarity theming is supposed to give you.

questions.question: Why run broad, phrase, and exact match versions of the same keyword in separate campaigns instead of the same ad group?
questions.optionA: Amazon technically forbids mixing match types in one ad group
questions.optionB: It gives independent budget and bid control per match type and avoids the same keyword competing against itself across match types
questions.optionC: Separate campaigns are required before Brand Registry approval
questions.optionD: It has no real effect — it's mainly a cosmetic organization choice
questions.explanation: Mixing match types in one ad group causes cannibalization: the same keyword in broad and exact can compete against itself in the auction. Separate campaigns by match type give you independent budgets and bids, and a clean read on which match type is actually performing.

questions.question: You've pulled 300 candidate keywords. Which two filtering criteria should you apply first, before scoring by volume or competition?
questions.optionA: Volume and competition
questions.optionB: Relevance and purchase intent
questions.optionC: Alphabetical order and keyword length
questions.optionD: Price and category
questions.explanation: Relevance and intent are the first cut: remove anything outside your product category and anything reflecting research intent ("how to," "vs," "review") before you spend time scoring what survives for volume and competition. Filtering by volume too early wastes scoring effort on keywords that should never have made the list.

quizzes.title: Listing Optimization Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of listing and ad relevance signals, listing anatomy, and A+ Content.

questions.question: Does Amazon expose a single named "Listing Quality Score" that a VA can look up directly?
questions.optionA: Yes, it's visible in Seller Central under Listing Quality
questions.optionB: No. Amazon doesn't publish a single inspectable score. CTR (click-through rate), CVR (conversion rate), and relevance are the observable signals instead
questions.optionC: Yes, but only for Brand Registry accounts
questions.optionD: No, because Amazon doesn't measure listing quality at all
questions.explanation: There's no single named, inspectable "Quality Score." Treat CTR, CVR, and relevance signals as the observable proxies for how well a listing is converting paid traffic, not a score you can pull from a report.

questions.question: Two listings for the same product get the same clicks. Listing A has a CVR (conversion rate) of 12.5% and a $0.52 CPC (cost per click). Listing B has a 6.1% CVR and an $0.89 CPC. Which gets more sales per ad dollar, and roughly by how much?
questions.optionA: Listing B, by about 2x
questions.optionB: They perform about the same
questions.optionC: Listing A, by about 3.5x
questions.optionD: Listing B, by about 3.5x
questions.explanation: Sales per ad dollar scales with CVR divided by CPC. (0.125 / 0.52) divided by (0.061 / 0.89) is about 3.5. A weaker listing doesn't just convert worse, it multiplies the gap because it's also paying more per click for the same targeting.

questions.question: Which of these listing elements has the most direct effect on whether a relevant click converts into a sale?
questions.optionA: The seller's account age
questions.optionB: Main images, title clarity, and review strength
questions.optionC: The campaign's daily budget
questions.optionD: The number of keywords targeted
questions.explanation: Once a shopper clicks through, it's the listing itself, images, title, bullets, reviews, and price, that decides whether they buy. Budget and keyword count affect whether you get the click, not what happens after.

questions.question: What does an ASIN identify?
questions.optionA: A seller's advertising account
questions.optionB: A specific product on Amazon
questions.optionC: A campaign's daily budget
questions.optionD: A shopper's search history
questions.explanation: ASIN (Amazon Standard Identification Number) is Amazon's product ID. Every distinct product listing has one.

questions.question: A seller without Brand Registry asks why it's worth enrolling. What's an accurate answer?
questions.optionA: Brand Registry guarantees a #1 search ranking
questions.optionB: It unlocks A+ Content and Sponsored Brands, which are commonly associated with better conversion and more ad placements, though exact lift varies by listing
questions.optionC: It's required before you're allowed to run any Sponsored Products campaign
questions.optionD: It removes Amazon's referral fees
questions.explanation: Brand Registry unlocks A+ Content and Sponsored Brands campaigns, both commonly linked to better conversion and reach. It's not a ranking guarantee, not required for basic Sponsored Products, and has nothing to do with referral fees.

questions.question: A listing's main image is 800px on a white background. What's the concrete problem?
questions.optionA: Nothing — white background is all that matters
questions.optionB: It's below the roughly 1000px minimum needed to enable Amazon's zoom feature
questions.optionC: Amazon will suspend the listing immediately
questions.optionD: The image needs a colored background instead
questions.explanation: Main images need to be at least around 1000px to enable Amazon's zoom feature, which listings commonly rely on to help shoppers examine the product before buying. White background is necessary but not sufficient on its own.

questions.question: A bullet point reads "350ml capacity." What's missing to make it a PPC-aware bullet?
questions.optionA: Nothing — specs are exactly what shoppers want to see
questions.optionB: The benefit and proof that turn the spec into a reason to buy
questions.optionC: A keyword-stuffed rewrite of the same spec
questions.optionD: An exclamation point for emphasis
questions.explanation: A bare feature like "350ml capacity" tells a shopper what the product is, not why it matters to them. The feature-to-benefit-to-proof structure turns a spec into a reason to click and buy.

questions.question: Why should a title stay concise and natural instead of stuffing in every possible keyword?
questions.optionA: Amazon enforces category-specific title-length limits, and a truncated or rejected title is worse than a clean, shorter one
questions.optionB: Longer titles always rank higher regardless of length limits
questions.optionC: Keyword stuffing has no downside as long as every word is relevant
questions.optionD: Amazon rewards keyword density with a lower CPC
questions.explanation: Amazon enforces hard title-length limits that vary by category and change over time. A title that gets truncated on mobile or rejected outright is a worse outcome than a shorter, natural title with the primary keyword near the front.

quizzes.title: Campaign Architecture Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of Sponsored Products, Sponsored Brands, Sponsored Display, and how to structure campaigns for maximum performance.

questions.question: Which Amazon ad type allows you to promote a portfolio of products with a custom headline and logo?
questions.optionA: Sponsored Products
questions.optionB: Sponsored Brands
questions.optionC: Sponsored Display
questions.optionD: Amazon DSP
questions.explanation: Sponsored Brands (formerly Headline Search Ads) feature your brand logo, a custom headline, and a collection of products. They appear at the top of search results and drive brand awareness.

questions.question: What is the primary advantage of a manual targeting campaign over auto campaigns?
questions.optionA: Manual campaigns are always cheaper
questions.optionB: Manual campaigns give you precise control over which keywords and match types you target
questions.optionC: Manual campaigns generate more impressions automatically
questions.optionD: Manual campaigns don't require any keyword research
questions.explanation: Manual targeting gives you explicit control over keyword selection and match types, allowing you to strategically bid on high-converting terms and exclude low-performers with precision.

questions.question: When should you use broad match keywords in your campaigns?
questions.optionA: When you want to discover new search terms that convert for your product
questions.optionB: When you want the most precise control over ad spend
questions.optionC: When you want to minimize irrelevant clicks
questions.optionD: Broad match should never be used in Amazon PPC
questions.explanation: Broad match is your discovery tool — it triggers your ad for variations and related searches, helping you find new converting search terms. Always monitor the search term report and convert high-performers to phrase or exact match.

questions.question: What is the recommended campaign structure for Sponsored Products?
questions.optionA: One campaign with all keywords in a single ad group
questions.optionB: Separate campaigns for auto, broad, phrase, and exact match types
questions.optionC: Only use auto campaigns — manual is too complicated
questions.optionD: One campaign per individual keyword
questions.explanation: Segmenting by match type (auto, broad, phrase, exact) into separate campaigns gives you granular budget and bid control at each stage of the keyword lifecycle — from discovery to optimization.

questions.question: Sponsored Display ads can target which of the following audiences?
questions.optionA: Only shoppers who searched for your exact keywords
questions.optionB: Views (shoppers who viewed your product) and Purchases (shoppers who bought your product)
questions.optionC: Only shoppers who added your product to cart
questions.optionD: Only shoppers on competing product detail pages
questions.explanation: Sponsored Display offers powerful remarketing: you can retarget shoppers who viewed your product (Views) or who purchased from you (Purchases) with different messaging strategies for each audience.

questions.question: What is a common mistake when setting daily budgets for multiple campaigns?
questions.optionA: Setting budgets too low, causing campaigns to pause mid-day and lose high-converting evening traffic
questions.optionB: Setting different budgets for different campaigns
questions.optionC: Using the same bid for all keywords in a campaign
questions.optionD: Running auto campaigns alongside manual campaigns
questions.explanation: Under-budgeting causes campaigns to stop running before the day ends. Amazon shoppers are active 24/7, and you may miss peak converting hours. Monitor spend patterns and set budgets that allow full-day coverage for proven campaigns.

questions.question: Your exact-match campaign already targets "garlic press" at a $1.10 bid with a proven 18% CVR. Your broad-match campaign for the same product is also picking up clicks on the same search term at a $0.35 bid. What fixes this?
questions.optionA: Raise the exact-match bid even higher to compensate
questions.optionB: Add "garlic press" as a negative exact keyword inside the broad-match campaign
questions.optionC: Delete the broad-match campaign entirely
questions.optionD: Lower the broad campaign's daily budget to zero
questions.explanation: Broad match naturally also matches the exact search it's meant to discover around, so both of your own campaigns end up eligible for the same search. Adding the term as a negative exact in the broad campaign stops it from competing with the exact campaign that already owns that keyword, freeing the broad campaign's budget for genuinely new terms.

questions.question: In the Campaign Builder tool's scoring, which criterion carries the most weight, and why?
questions.optionA: Keyword selection, because relevance matters more than anything else
questions.optionB: Campaign structure, because a well-organized campaign with decent keywords outperforms a chaotic campaign with great keywords
questions.optionC: Negative keywords, because wasted spend is the single biggest risk
questions.optionD: Budget allocation, because the campaign with the most money always wins
questions.explanation: Campaign structure carries the most weight (30%) because it's the foundation everything else depends on. Good keywords and reasonable bids can't do their job inside a structure that mixes proven and unproven terms in the same budget and ad group.

quizzes.title: Portfolio Strategy Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of campaign portfolios, budget pacing, and seasonal strategy.

questions.question: At roughly what campaign count does it make sense to move from managing campaigns individually to grouping them into portfolios?
questions.optionA: 2-3 campaigns
questions.optionB: 10 or more campaigns
questions.optionC: 100 or more campaigns
questions.optionD: Never — always manage every campaign individually
questions.explanation: Below roughly 10 campaigns, managing each one individually is still practical. Past that point, shared budgeting and consolidated reporting through portfolios save real time.

questions.question: A portfolio has a ₱60,000 monthly budget. Campaigns inside it have spent ₱57,000 combined with a few days left in the month. What happens once the portfolio's ₱60,000 is fully spent?
questions.optionA: Only the highest-spending campaign inside the portfolio pauses
questions.optionB: Every campaign inside the portfolio stops serving for the rest of the period, regardless of each one's own remaining budget
questions.optionC: The portfolio automatically raises its own budget to keep campaigns running
questions.optionD: Nothing — portfolio budgets are informational only and don't cap spend
questions.explanation: A portfolio budget is a spend cap for the whole group over the period. Once it's exhausted, every campaign inside stops serving, even one that still had room left on its own individual budget.

questions.question: Do negative keywords and bid adjustments apply across every campaign in a portfolio automatically?
questions.optionA: Yes — portfolios manage negatives and bids for every campaign inside them
questions.optionB: No — negatives and bid adjustments are campaign-level controls, so each campaign in a portfolio still needs its own
questions.optionC: Only bids are shared across the portfolio, not negatives
questions.optionD: Only negatives are shared across the portfolio, not bids
questions.explanation: Portfolios group campaigns for shared budgeting and reporting only. Negative keywords and bid adjustments stay campaign-level, so a new campaign added to a portfolio still needs its own negative list built or copied over.

questions.question: A campaign with a ₱1,500 daily budget has spent 80% of it by 11AM, three days running. What does this pattern indicate, and what's the fix?
questions.optionA: Normal pacing — no action needed
questions.optionB: Budget is too low for demand; raise the daily budget
questions.optionC: Budget is too high for demand; lower it
questions.optionD: The campaign should be paused immediately
questions.explanation: A good pacing target is 80-90% of the daily budget spent by end of day. Hitting 80% by 11AM repeatedly means the campaign is burning through budget in a few hours and going dark for the rest of the day — a sign to raise the budget, not a curiosity to ignore.

questions.question: Over what period is Amazon's stated daily budget actually averaged, and what does that mean for a single day's spend?
questions.optionA: Averaged over the calendar month; a single day can legitimately spend above the daily budget, up to an account-set over-delivery cap
questions.optionB: Averaged over a single week only
questions.optionC: It's a hard per-day cap that can never be exceeded
questions.optionD: Averaged over the product's entire lifetime on Amazon
questions.explanation: The daily budget is averaged over the calendar month, and Amazon allows a single high-traffic day to spend above that average, capped at either 25% or 100% over depending on the account's setting, as long as the month's total doesn't exceed daily budget times days in the month.

questions.question: ACoS rises from 20% to 32% during a seasonal push while margin stays flat and ad spend grows substantially. What should decide whether this is actually a problem?
questions.optionA: ACoS alone — any increase is a red flag that should be reversed
questions.optionB: Whether profit after ad spend (sales times margin, minus ad spend) still increases despite the higher ACoS
questions.optionC: Whether the client feels nervous about the number
questions.optionD: The absolute peso size of the ad spend increase, regardless of sales
questions.explanation: A higher ACoS during a seasonal push is expected and can still mean more money for the client, as long as the sales-volume increase outpaces the efficiency drop. Profit after ad spend is the number that actually answers whether the trade-off is worth it, not ACoS on its own.

questions.question: Per this module's seasonal calendar, when should Q4 (Christmas) PPC preparation start?
questions.optionA: October 1, when Q4 officially begins
questions.optionB: August, roughly two months ahead of the peak spending window
questions.optionC: The day after Black Friday
questions.optionD: Whenever the client happens to remember to ask
questions.explanation: Christmas prep starts in August: researching seasonal keywords, launching discovery campaigns, and testing seasonal messaging well before the November-December peak window.

questions.question: A seasonal profit-after-ad-spend calculation assumes margin stays flat between a normal month and a promotional month. What should you check before trusting that calculation?
questions.optionA: Nothing — margin never changes seasonally
questions.optionB: Whether the seller is running discounts or lower prices during the promotional push, which would lower the actual margin used in the calculation
questions.optionC: Whether the client has approved the calculation in writing
questions.optionD: Whether ACoS stays below 50% throughout the season
questions.explanation: Sellers often discount or run promotions during peak season, which lowers the actual margin. A profit-after-ad-spend projection built on a flat margin assumption needs to be redone with the real promotional margin, not treated as guaranteed.

quizzes.title: Portfolio Strategy Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of campaign portfolios, budget pacing, and seasonal strategy — the account-level skills for managing scale.

questions.question: At what rough campaign count does this module recommend switching from managing campaigns individually to grouping them into portfolios?
questions.optionA: 2-3 campaigns
questions.optionB: Around 10 or more campaigns
questions.optionC: Only after 100+ campaigns
questions.optionD: Never — always manage each campaign individually
questions.explanation: Once an account has roughly 10 or more campaigns, group them into portfolios for shared budgeting and reporting. Below that, managing campaigns one by one is still practical.

questions.question: Using the 60/20/10/10 rule on a ₱100,000/month budget, how much goes to the New Launches portfolio?
questions.explanation: New Launches gets 20% of the budget under the 60/20/10/10 rule: 20% of ₱100,000 is ₱20,000. Core Products gets 60%, Brand Defense and Seasonal each get 10%.

questions.question: Do negative keywords automatically apply across every campaign inside a portfolio?
questions.optionA: Yes, portfolios maintain one shared negative list for every campaign inside them
questions.optionB: No — negative keywords and bid adjustments are campaign-level controls, so each campaign needs its own
questions.optionC: Only for Sponsored Brands campaigns
questions.optionD: Only if a shared-negatives setting is turned on for the portfolio
questions.explanation: Portfolios group campaigns for shared budgeting and reporting, but they don't carry a shared negative-keyword list. Each campaign inside a portfolio still needs its own negatives entered or copied over.

questions.question: What's a good pacing target for the percentage of a daily budget spent by end of day?
questions.optionD: Exactly 100% by noon
questions.explanation: A good pacing target is 80 to 90% of the daily budget spent by end of day. Hitting 100% by midday is a signal the budget is too low for demand, not a target to aim for.

questions.question: Over how long a period is your Amazon daily budget actually averaged, and what can happen on a single high-traffic day?
questions.optionA: Averaged over a single day; spend can never exceed 100% of the daily budget
questions.optionB: Averaged over the calendar month; a single day can over-deliver by up to 25% or up to 100%, depending on the account's setting
questions.optionC: Averaged over a calendar year with no daily limit at all
questions.optionD: Averaged over the campaign's total lifetime, with a fixed spend per day
questions.explanation: Amazon's daily budget is an average across the calendar month, not a hard per-day cap. A single day can legitimately show 125% or 200% of the daily budget depending on which over-delivery setting (25% or 100%) is active on the account.

questions.question: During a Q4 peak, a campaign's ACoS rises from 25% to 40%, but profit after ad spend increases by ₱25,000. What's the correct read?
questions.optionA: The campaign is failing because ACoS went up
questions.optionB: Rising ACoS during a peak event can be acceptable if profit after ad spend still increases because sales volume grew enough to offset the lower efficiency
questions.optionC: ACoS and profit after ad spend always move in the same direction
questions.optionD: Profit after ad spend and ACoS measure the same thing
questions.explanation: Judge a seasonal campaign by whether profit after ad spend is going up, not by whether ACoS is going up. A higher ACoS during a peak event is expected and can still mean more money for the client if sales volume grows enough.

questions.question: When should Q4 holiday-season preparation start, according to this module?
questions.optionA: October 1st, right when the season begins
questions.optionB: August, roughly two months before the October start of the peak
questions.optionC: The week of Black Friday
questions.optionD: Only after Q3 sales numbers come in
questions.explanation: Start Q4 preparation in August: research seasonal keywords, launch discovery campaigns, and test seasonal ad copy well before the October-December peak, not once it has already started.

quizzes.title: Bidding Lab Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Verify your understanding of bid strategies, placement adjustments, and how to optimize bids for profitability.

questions.question: What does 'Dynamic Bids - Down Only' do?
questions.optionA: Automatically increases your bid for placements likely to convert
questions.optionB: Automatically decreases your bid for placements unlikely to convert, but never raises it
questions.optionC: Sets all your bids to the same amount
questions.optionD: Dynamically adjusts bids based on time of day
questions.explanation: Dynamic Bids - Down Only tells Amazon to reduce your bid when the placement is unlikely to convert, saving you money on low-value clicks. It never raises your bid above your set amount, making it the most conservative strategy.

questions.question: You're running a campaign with 50% placement adjustment for 'Top of Search'. If your default bid is $1.00, what is your maximum bid for top of search?
questions.explanation: A 50% placement adjustment increases your bid by 50% for that placement: $1.00 + ($1.00 × 0.50) = $1.50 maximum bid for top of search positions.

questions.question: When should you use 'Dynamic Bids - Up and Down'?
questions.optionA: When you want to minimize ad spend at all costs
questions.optionB: When your campaigns are profitable and you want Amazon to increase bids for high-conversion opportunities
questions.optionC: Only for auto campaigns
questions.optionD: When launching a new campaign with no historical data
questions.explanation: Up and Down bidding works best on proven campaigns with good ACoS. Amazon will raise bids for placements likely to convert and lower them for poor ones. Avoid it on new or unprofitable campaigns.

questions.question: What is the risk of setting your default bid too high in a manual campaign?
questions.optionA: Your ads won't show at all
questions.optionB: You may win clicks for expensive, low-converting search terms and rapidly drain your budget
questions.optionC: Amazon will automatically lower your bid
questions.optionD: Your ACoS will decrease automatically
questions.explanation: Overbidding wins you more auctions — including low-quality ones. You'll burn through budget on expensive clicks from irrelevant or low-converting search terms, driving up ACoS and reducing overall profitability.

questions.question: Your keyword has a CPC of $2.50, CVR of 8%, and your product price is $30 with 30% profit margin. What is your approximate ACoS?
questions.explanation: Cost per order = CPC / CVR = $2.50 / 0.08 = $31.25. ACoS = Ad Spend / Ad Revenue = $31.25 / $30 = 104.2%. Since this exceeds 100%, you're paying more per order than the product price — this keyword is extremely unprofitable.

questions.question: A $1.00 base bid uses Dynamic Up and Down at its maximum +100% increase, stacked with a +900% top-of-search placement adjustment. What's the maximum possible effective bid at top of search?
questions.optionA: $1.00, since placement adjustments replace the dynamic increase rather than stacking with it
questions.optionB: $10.00, from the placement adjustment alone
questions.optionC: $20.00, since the two multipliers stack: $1.00 × 2.0 × 10.0
questions.optionD: $2.00, from the dynamic increase alone
questions.explanation: Dynamic bid adjustments and placement adjustments stack multiplicatively, not additively. At their combined maximum, a $1.00 base bid can become $1.00 × 2.0 (dynamic) × 10.0 (placement) = $20.00, a 20x multiplier that catches advertisers who only account for one of the two.

questions.question: A keyword's market CPC range sits entirely above your calculated max CPC for the target ACoS. What are your real options?
questions.optionA: Bid above your max CPC anyway, since high competition means the keyword must be worth it
questions.optionB: Accept a higher ACoS, improve CVR through listing work, or walk away from the keyword
questions.optionC: Always walk away — there's never a reason to bid above your calculated max CPC
questions.optionD: Switch to Dynamic Up and Down, which removes the ceiling entirely
questions.explanation: Good bidding is as much about walking away as picking a number. When the market won't let you win profitably at your target ACoS, the real choices are accepting a higher ACoS (sometimes defensible, like during a launch), improving conversion rate so the same CPC supports a lower ACoS, or not bidding on that keyword at all — not bidding blind above your ceiling.

quizzes.title: Search Term Triage Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of search term analysis, negative keywords, and how to optimize campaigns through strategic triage decisions.

questions.question: What is a search term in Amazon PPC?
questions.optionA: The keyword you bid on in your campaign
questions.optionB: The actual shopper query that triggered your ad
questions.optionC: The title of your product listing
questions.optionD: The search algorithm Amazon uses
questions.explanation: A search term is the actual query a shopper typed — which may differ from your keyword. For example, if you bid on the broad keyword 'water bottle', a search term might be 'insulated water bottle for gym'. This distinction is critical for optimization.

questions.question: When should you add a search term as an exact negative keyword?
questions.optionA: When the term has high spend and zero sales
questions.optionB: When the term has a high ACoS above your target
questions.optionC: When the term is completely irrelevant to your product
questions.optionD: All of the above are valid reasons
questions.explanation: All three scenarios justify adding an exact negative: high spend with zero sales is pure waste, ACoS above target means the term is unprofitable, and completely irrelevant terms waste budget and hurt CTR.

questions.question: What is the difference between negative exact and negative phrase match types?
questions.optionA: They work the same way for negatives
questions.optionB: Negative exact blocks only that specific search term; negative phrase blocks the term and any searches containing it
questions.optionC: Negative phrase is more restrictive than negative exact
questions.optionD: There is no phrase match option for negatives
questions.explanation: Negative exact match blocks your ad from showing for only that specific search term. Negative phrase match blocks your ad for any search that contains the term, which is broader. Use negative exact for precision and negative phrase to block entire categories of unwanted searches.

questions.question: A search term has 500 impressions, 2 clicks, and 0 orders with $3.50 spend. What triage action should you consider?
questions.optionA: Keep bidding — it might convert with more clicks
questions.optionB: Increase your bid to get more visibility
questions.optionC: Add as a negative keyword — the CTR is very low and it's spending without converting
questions.optionD: Do nothing — 2 clicks is not enough data
questions.explanation: CTR of 0.4% (2/500) is extremely low and the term has $3.50 spend with zero return. This indicates the search term is irrelevant to your product. Adding it as a negative prevents further waste.

questions.question: You find a high-converting search term in your broad match campaign. What is the recommended next step?
questions.optionA: Leave it in the broad campaign and increase the broad bid
questions.optionB: Add it as an exact match keyword in a separate exact campaign with a higher bid
questions.optionC: Remove it from the broad campaign immediately
questions.optionD: Add it as a negative keyword to prevent broad from triggering for it
questions.explanation: The best practice is to graduate high-converting search terms to an exact match campaign with a higher bid. This gives you precise control and ensures you win auctions for this proven term. Optionally, add it as a negative in the broad campaign to avoid competing with yourself.

questions.question: Why is regular search term analysis essential for PPC profitability?
questions.optionA: Amazon requires weekly reports to keep your account active
questions.optionB: It helps you discover irrelevant terms wasting budget and find new converting terms to target explicitly
questions.optionC: It automatically optimizes your bids for you
questions.optionD: It replaces the need for bid strategy adjustments
questions.explanation: Regular search term analysis is the single highest-ROI activity in PPC management. It lets you cut waste (irrelevant terms draining budget) and capture opportunity (converting terms you should bid on explicitly). This is the core loop: discover → triage → optimize → repeat.

questions.question: A search term has 3 clicks and 1 order, a 33% CVR. Why shouldn't you treat this as proof the term is a strong converter?
questions.optionA: 3 clicks is too small a sample to trust; the true conversion rate could be very different once more data comes in
questions.optionB: 33% CVR is mathematically impossible, so the data must be wrong
questions.optionC: You should always wait exactly 100 clicks before taking any action on any term
questions.optionD: Low click counts always mean the term is irrelevant
questions.explanation: A handful of clicks can produce an eye-catching CVR by pure chance. Confidence grows with volume: below 30 clicks your CVR estimate carries a wide margin of error, and it's much tighter above 100 clicks. A 33% CVR on 3 clicks is one lucky order, not a proven pattern yet.

questions.question: You rank #2 organically for a keyword your Sponsored Products ad also targets. A shopper who would have found you organically clicks the paid ad instead. What category does this fall into, and what should you check?
questions.optionA: Winner — any click that converts should be harvested and bid up further
questions.optionB: Cannibalizer — check whether the ad click is incremental or just paying for traffic you'd have gotten for free
questions.optionC: Irrelevant — negative the term immediately
questions.optionD: Surprise — investigate it as a new keyword opportunity
questions.explanation: This is the Cannibalizer category: you may be paying for a click you'd have earned organically anyway. The judgment call is whether the ad is bringing in incremental shoppers (good) or just displacing free organic clicks (wasted spend) — worth reducing bids on if you rank highly, and worth keeping if your organic position is weak.

quizzes.title: Competitive Intelligence Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of Brand Analytics, share of voice, and competitor benchmarking.

questions.question: What does Amazon Brand Analytics' Search Frequency Rank actually tell you about a search term?
questions.optionA: The exact number of monthly searches for that term
questions.optionB: A relative ranking against every other search term in the period — rank 1 is the most-searched, but the gap between ranks isn't a fixed size
questions.optionC: How many advertisers are currently bidding on that term
questions.optionD: The term's average CPC across the category
questions.explanation: Search Frequency Rank is relative, not absolute. Rank 1 is the single most-searched term in the period, and higher numbers mean less popular, but Amazon doesn't disclose actual search counts, and the gap between rank 5 and 6 isn't the same size as between rank 100 and 101.

questions.question: Per this lesson, what does a seller need beyond Brand Registry enrollment to actually access Amazon Brand Analytics?
questions.optionA: Nothing more — Brand Registry enrollment alone is sufficient
questions.optionB: An active Professional selling account and Brand Representative access assigned for the enrolled brand
questions.optionC: At least $10,000 in monthly ad spend
questions.optionD: A minimum of 100 product reviews
questions.explanation: Brand Registry enrollment alone isn't enough to see Brand Analytics. The account also needs an active Professional selling account and Brand Representative access assigned for that brand — confirm both before promising a client this data.

questions.question: Share of voice measures which of the following?
questions.optionA: How much a brand spends on advertising in total dollars
questions.optionB: A brand's visibility relative to competitors for a given keyword or category, not an absolute spend figure
questions.optionC: The number of five-star reviews a product has
questions.optionD: How many Sponsored Brands campaigns an account is running
questions.explanation: Share of voice is a relative visibility measure — how often a brand shows up for a keyword or category compared to competitors — not a dollar figure or a review count.

questions.question: A gap analysis dimension shows competitors averaging 2.5 (Strong/Medium) and you averaging 1.0 (Weak). Using the matrix's scoring rule (Opportunity = competitors' average at or below 1.5 and yours at or above 2; Vulnerability = competitors' average at or above 2 and yours at or below 1.5), what does this dimension represent?
questions.optionA: Opportunity — double down since you're clearly ahead of competitors here
questions.optionB: Vulnerability — competitors are strong here and you're weak, so this needs shoring up
questions.optionC: Neither — this dimension needs no action
questions.optionD: Not enough information — the four-point scale doesn't apply to this dimension
questions.explanation: This clears the vulnerability rule exactly: competitors' average (2.5) is at or above 2, and your average (1.0) is at or below 1.5. That combination means competitors are winning where you're weak — a gap to shore up, not one to leave for later.

quizzes.title: Competitive Intelligence Knowledge Check
quizzes.description: Test your understanding of Brand Analytics, Share of Voice, and competitor benchmarking — turning competitive data into specific campaign actions.

questions.question: What do you need, beyond Brand Registry enrollment, to access Amazon Brand Analytics (ABA)?
questions.optionA: Nothing else — Brand Registry enrollment alone unlocks ABA
questions.optionB: An active Professional selling account and Brand Representative access assigned for that brand
questions.optionC: A minimum of ₱500,000/month in ad spend
questions.optionD: Enrollment in Amazon DSP
questions.explanation: Brand Registry enrollment alone isn't enough to see ABA. The account also needs an active Professional selling account and Brand Representative access assigned for that brand.

questions.question: Amazon discontinued the standalone Item Comparison / Alternate Purchase Behavior report in 2022. How do you find competitor ASINs to target now?
questions.optionA: It's impossible without third-party tools
questions.optionB: Use the top-clicked ASINs shown in the Top Search Terms report, plus Market Basket Analysis
questions.optionC: Amazon emails a list of competitor ASINs automatically
questions.optionD: Competitor ASINs can only be found through Sponsored Display
questions.explanation: Competitor ASIN discovery now comes from Top Search Terms' top-clicked products, Market Basket Analysis, and your own search-based research, not a dedicated comparison report.

questions.question: Your demographics report shows mostly high-income buyers. Does that alone justify raising your ACoS ceiling for that segment?
questions.optionA: Yes, high income always means a higher acceptable ACoS
questions.optionB: No — demographics are a targeting hypothesis; the ACoS ceiling should still come from margin and this segment's measured performance
questions.optionC: Yes, but only for luxury products
questions.optionD: No, demographics reports are unreliable and should be ignored entirely
questions.explanation: Demographics data is a targeting hypothesis, not proof of conversion or profitability. Set your ACoS ceiling from margin and this segment's actual measured performance, not income alone.

questions.question: Amazon doesn't give you total category impression data directly. What should you do to estimate Share of Voice (SOV)?
questions.optionA: Wait for Amazon to publish an official SOV report
questions.optionB: Build an estimate using Brand Analytics, campaign reports, or a bid-ceiling test
questions.optionC: Assume your SOV is always 50%
questions.optionD: SOV can't be estimated without third-party software
questions.explanation: Treat SOV as an estimate you build, not a report you pull. Brand Analytics' Top Search Terms, your own campaign reports, or a small bid-ceiling test are the three ways to approximate it.

questions.question: Your SOV for a keyword is 40%. What's the right strategic move?
questions.optionA: Keep raising bids to grow impression share further
questions.optionB: Shift budget toward ROAS and new segments, since you're already in the Dominant tier
questions.optionC: Pause the keyword since SOV is too high
questions.optionD: SOV over 35% means you should lower your price instead
questions.explanation: Above 35% SOV you're Dominant. The right posture is maximizing ROAS and shifting budget to new segments, not continuing to chase more impression share you've already won.

questions.question: Your SOV on a keyword drops 12% in one week. How fast should you investigate?
questions.optionA: Wait for the monthly review
questions.optionB: Immediately — a 10%+ weekly drop is a signal to investigate right away
questions.optionC: Only if it keeps dropping for three consecutive months
questions.optionD: SOV drops don't need investigation, only rises do
questions.explanation: A 10%+ SOV drop in a week is an alert, not something to file for the monthly review. Investigate immediately — it could be a budget issue or a new competitor entering the market.

questions.question: In the gap analysis matrix, competitors average 2.5 on a dimension and you average 1.0. What does this indicate?
questions.optionA: An opportunity to double down
questions.optionB: A vulnerability to shore up
questions.optionC: A contested dimension needing a closer look
questions.optionD: Data that should be ignored
questions.explanation: Vulnerability = competitors' average at or above 2 AND your average at or below 1.5. Competitors at 2.5 and you at 1.0 clears that rule, flagging a gap to shore up before scaling anything else.

questions.question: Where does "new product launches" fit on the gap analysis matrix's Strong/Medium/Weak/Not-using scale?
questions.optionA: It's always scored Strong for whoever launches fastest
questions.optionB: It doesn't fit the scale — it's tracked as a separate qualitative note instead
questions.optionC: It's scored the same way as brand term defense
questions.optionD: New product launches are excluded from competitive analysis entirely
questions.explanation: Speed to market is a different thing from execution quality — a competitor can launch fast and badly, or slowly and well. Track it as a qualitative note rather than forcing it into the four-point score.
